analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' windfall heating-oil profits at 90% to fund low-income heating aid.
analysis.headline: The windfall-profits bill, backed by 25 House members from both parties, never got a hearing or vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After heating oil prices jumped in late 1989, this bill would have taxed away 90% of the extra profit home heating oil producers and importers earned above their average profit in November 1989. The money would go into a new Home Heating Oil Trust Fund and be spent on Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) grants that help poor households pay winter heating bills. It applied to sales after November 1989 and required producers to pay twice a month. The bill was sent to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that struggle to pay heating bills: up to $300 million in the first fiscal year would flow to LIHEAP heating grants without needing a separate appropriation, funded directly by the windfall tax [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households facing high heating bills

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 90% excise tax on the windfall profit from each barrel of home heating oil — the profit above the producer's or importer's average gross profit per barrel in November 1989, before the price spike [S2][S3].
Creates a Home Heating Oil Trust Fund receiving all the tax revenue, dedicated to LIHEAP grants, with up to $300 million available in fiscal 1990 without a further appropriation [S2][S3].

Applies to all sales after November 30, 1989, including December 1989 itself, so the tax captures the profits earned during the initial price spike; related-party sales are valued at fair market value to prevent shifting profits between affiliates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Home heating oil producers and importers, who would hand over 90% of the profit they earned above their November 1989 baseline; some of that cost could be passed forward in prices, and the tax could dull the incentive to bring heating oil to market during a shortage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Home heating oil producers and importers

drawbacks.text: A windfall tax on producers and importers can weaken their incentive to produce or import heating oil when it is scarcest, which could tighten supply and push prices up for the very households the aid targets [S3].

The tax uses a single baseline month (November 1989) and applies to every quarter after December 1989, so it could keep taxing ordinary margins long after any windfall ended if prices stayed elevated; narrow baselines in windfall-profits taxes are hard to calibrate [S3].

Because the tax falls on gross profit over a baseline, it does not adjust for producers whose costs rose differently, and firms that barely sold in November 1989 get an IRS-set national average baseline instead of their own history [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a direct trade: claw back most of the extra profits refiners and importers earned from a price spike and turn that money into heating grants for poor households. That is a strong deal for working families during a winter price shock. The honest costs are real but secondary: windfall taxes can discourage supply during shortages and a fixed November 1989 baseline is a blunt measuring stick. On balance, the design was targeted (a windfall is profit above a baseline, not all profit) and the aid was automatic for the first year.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Silvio Conte (R-MA) introduced the bill on January 23, 1990, joined by nine other original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The bill attracted 24 cosponsors in total — 16 House Democrats and 8 House Republicans — but no further action of any kind was taken after the referral [S4][S5].
The Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law, held no hearing or markup, and the full House never voted on the bill before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home heating oil producers and importers kept 100% of their windfall profits from the 1989-90 price spike, and low-income households got no additional heating aid from this source. The Ways and Means Committee never had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers kept the windfall; no new heating aid

for.name: Rep. Silvio O. Conte
for.what_they_did: Introduced the windfall profits tax and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 8 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Shays, Neal, and Smith of Vermont.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican lead sponsor with 24 cosponsors split 16 Democrats to 8 Republicans — so the bill's death in committee was not a party-line fight.

industries.industry: Home heating oil producers and importers
industries.note: The bill would take 90% of profits they earned above their November 1989 baseline during a heating-oil price spike, effectively refunding the windfall to poor households. Keeping those profits meant higher effective costs for consumers paying spiked prices.

industries.industry: LIHEAP grantees (states and local community-action agencies)
industries.note: A dedicated trust fund would have added up to $300 million in fiscal 1990 for heating assistance grants, without a new appropriation. The bill died, so the funding never arrived.
